title: Alerting & On-Call Design
summary: Designing alerts around what users actually feel, not every possible internal cause, so paging stays meaningful instead of constant noise.

slides.markdown:
Metrics and logs are useless at 3am if nobody's looking at them — **alerting** is what turns observability data into a human getting paged. Done well, it wakes someone up only when users are actually affected. Done badly, it pages for every internal blip until everyone mutes it.

This topic covers alerting on symptoms instead of causes, setting thresholds that hold up under real noise, and the alert-fatigue spiral that makes on-call miserable and, eventually, unsafe.

slides.sectionTitle: Alert on symptoms (user impact), not every possible cause
slides.markdown:
A **symptom-based alert** fires on user-visible impact — "checkout success rate dropped below 99%." A **cause-based alert** fires on a specific internal condition that *might* lead to impact — "database connection pool at 80% utilization," "one of twelve replicas is down."

The problem with cause-based alerting at scale is that there are far more possible causes than possible symptoms, and most causes never actually produce user-visible harm — a single replica dying in a healthy twelve-replica cluster is a non-event if the other eleven absorb the load fine. Alerting on every cause means paging for things that don't matter, which is exactly how alert fatigue starts.

The rule of thumb: page on symptoms; use cause-level signals as the diagnostic layer you check *after* a symptom alert fires, not as separate pages.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: symptom-based alert vs cause-based alert, same incident
slides.markdown:
![Cause-based alerts versus one symptom-based alert](assets/alert-design-comparison.svg)

The same underlying incident produces three ambiguous cause-based pages, each individually unclear whether it matters, versus one unambiguous symptom-based page that directly says users are affected. The on-call engineer investigating the symptom alert would then look at the cause-level signals as context, not as three separate 3am interruptions.

slides.sectionTitle: Setting thresholds that catch real problems without noise
slides.markdown:
A threshold set too tight fires on normal variance — a 2% error-rate alert on a service that normally blips to 1.8% during deploys will page constantly for nothing. A threshold set too loose misses real problems — a 50% error-rate alert won't fire until the outage is already severe.

Good thresholds come from looking at the metric's real historical distribution, not a guessed round number: find what "normal" actually looks like, including its normal spikes, and set the threshold clearly above that noise floor. Pairing a threshold with a duration ("error rate above 5% for 5 minutes," not "for one data point") filters out single-sample blips without meaningfully delaying detection of a real, sustained problem.

slides.sectionTitle: Alert fatigue: what happens when everything pages
slides.markdown:
**Alert fatigue** sets in when an on-call engineer gets paged often enough for non-actionable things that the response to any page, real or not, becomes "probably nothing." Once that mindset takes hold, a genuinely critical page gets the same delayed, half-attentive response as the ninety noise pages before it — the exact opposite of what paging exists for.

The fix isn't a mindset change, it's structural: every alert should be actionable (there's something a human can actually do about it right now) and every non-actionable-but-worth-tracking signal should go to a dashboard or ticket queue instead of a page. An alert that nobody can act on shouldn't wake anyone up.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: paging alerts vs ticket-queue alerts vs dashboards-only
slides.markdown:
| | Paging | Ticket queue | Dashboard-only |
|---|---|---|---|
| Urgency | Needs a human right now | Needs attention, not urgently | No action implied, just visibility |
| Example | Checkout success rate collapse | Disk usage trending toward full in 2 weeks | Daily active users, general traffic trend |
| Cost of over-using | Alert fatigue, burned-out on-call | Backlog nobody triages | None, but under-used it hides real problems |

**How to decide:** ask "does a human need to act in the next few minutes, or is this informational/trend-level?" — page only for the first, ticket for the second, dashboard for everything else. Misrouting a dashboard-level signal to paging is the single most common source of unnecessary on-call pain.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: an alert that fires constantly and gets silently muted
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We have an alert for that, so we'd catch it."

**Why it's wrong:** an alert that fires too often for non-actionable reasons doesn't get fixed — it gets muted, snoozed, or routed to a channel nobody reads, usually quietly and without a ticket to revisit it. The alert still technically "exists," but it has stopped protecting anyone months before someone notices.

**Correct model:** treat a high-noise alert as a bug to fix immediately, not tolerate — tighten the threshold, add a duration requirement, or delete it if it can't be made actionable. An alert's existence on paper means nothing if its real-world signal-to-noise ratio has already pushed everyone to ignore it.

slides.sectionTitle: Burn-rate alerting: paging based on how fast you're spending an SLO's error budget
slides.markdown:
A raw "error rate above X%" threshold treats a brief, sharp spike and a mild, sustained elevation as equally alert-worthy, even though they consume a monthly error budget at very different rates. **Burn-rate alerting** instead asks: at the current error rate, how fast is the service consuming its allowed error budget for the period?

Say a service has a 99.9% monthly availability SLO — a 0.1% error budget for the month. A burn rate of 1x means errors are accumulating exactly fast enough to exhaust the whole month's budget by month's end, which is fine, arguably expected. A burn rate of 14x, common in real burn-rate alert configs, means the current error rate would exhaust the entire monthly budget in about 2 days if it continued — that's worth waking someone up for, even though the instantaneous error rate might look modest in isolation.

Production SLO alerting typically layers **multiple windows** (a fast 1-hour window catching sudden severe burn, plus a slower 6-hour window catching sustained moderate burn), so both a sharp spike and a slow leak get caught, each at the urgency their actual budget consumption warrants.

slides.sectionTitle: Escalation policies and runbooks: what happens after the page fires
slides.markdown:
A page firing is the start of the response, not the end of the design work. An **escalation policy** defines what happens if the first on-call engineer doesn't acknowledge within a set window (commonly 5-15 minutes): page a secondary, then a team lead, then a wider incident channel — so a single missed page (phone on silent, in the shower) doesn't leave a real incident unattended indefinitely.

A **runbook** attached to the alert turns "something's wrong" into "here's what to check first" — the specific dashboards to open, the most common root causes for this exact alert, and the safe first mitigations (like a rollback or a feature-flag toggle) before deep debugging starts. An alert with no runbook forces every on-call engineer to rediscover the same diagnostic steps from scratch, often at 3am, which is exactly when the cost of that rediscovery is highest.

Together, these two pieces are what keep alerting effective under real-world imperfection — humans miss pages, and even a good engineer is slower and more error-prone half-asleep than a runbook written calmly in daylight.
